Not quite. They are essentially hosting a site that has links uploaded by the users. These links contain files (hosted by other sites), torrent files. These torrent files allow the user to connect with people who already own the content, and each person sharing the content (seed) gives a small portion of the file to the person who wants the file (leech).

So each individual seed is essentially sharing a small portion of the file with someone who doesn't have it. The issue becomes, when is sharing theft?

In the 80s, individuals would copy cassettes and, later, VHS tapes for their friends. Was this piracy? Was this sharing? Now, it's done on a massive, international scale with little-to-no loss in quality. When did it stop being sharing and start being theft? What should be the legal limit?

Additionally, should people pay for content, only to receive advertising tagged along with their content? Should people pay for an album when they only want a single? Will the existing mediums even pay the artists (iTunes is infamous for this, even occasionally selling people's music without their permission!)?

As you can see, the issue gets complicated and convoluted, but that's a rough summary.
This will also probably help set some legal precedent that will protect such ventures in the future, but yes this also means "we don't have sufficient evidence to successfully prosecute."

It was a lack of proof, not a question of law that got these guys off the hook.

Unusually, the case was based in criminal law, with Svartholm, Neij, Sunde and Lundström all standing accused of a range of crimes including criminal copyright infringement and abuse of electronic communications. However, the case itself has always experienced problems.

All four defendants deny having had anything to do with the site since its reported sale to a Seychelles-based company called Reservella in 2006. That has proven problematic, since the period in which the four allegedly committed the crimes detailed in the Belgian case spans September 2011 and November 2013.

Having failed to connect the quartet with the site’s operations during that period, the case has now fallen apart. Yesterday a judge at the Mechelse Court ruled that it could not be proven that the four were involved in the site during the period in question.
